newsitem.title: CANADA: ADM deal with UGG seen with eye on Wheat Board.
newsitem.headline: ADM deal with UGG seen with eye on Wheat Board.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co.'s decision to buy a 45 percent stake in Canada's second largest grain handler was likely done with an eye on the fate of the Canadian Wheat Board, industry analysts said.

"This is obviously some long-term planning. They're assuming they won't have to deal with the Canadian Wheat Board in five or 10 years," University of Manitoba agriculture economist Daryl Kraft said Friday.

Winnipeg-based United Grain Growers Ltd. announced the C$113 million ($82 million) deal with Decatur, Ill.,-based ADM Thursday, the latest in a string of merger deals for ADM that have made it the second-largest grain merchant in the United States after Cargill Inc.
"Clearly, they'd like to control the grain without having to negotiate with an intermediary," Kraft said.
The Canadian Wheat Board -- a state trading company with a monopoly on exports of barley and wheat from western Canada -- has been under attack in recent years from many quarters.

Canadian farmers, private grain companies like United Grain Growers, U.S. farm lobbies and even one political party aiming to form Canada's next federal government in Monday's national vote have all criticised the Wheat Board's monopoly powers.
More than 20,000 farmers voted to strike down the board's single-desk monopoly sales of barley in a plebiscite in March, but 63 percent of the 57,000 voters voted to retain the board.
Canadian Wheat Board opponents have said they will continue pressure for the option to sell grain outside traditional board channels.
"We see the Canadian industry becoming less regulated and more dynamic," United Grain Growers President Ted Allen said. "This alliance gives us a link to one of the biggest end-users in the world."
The ADM deal is subject to a shareholder vote July 17.

"Our decisions are based on the current business environment," ADM Vice President Martin Andreas told reporters Thursday. "We're interested in doing more processing in Canada. We think there's going to be considerable growth in exports."

Such winds of change have attracted more U.S. agribusiness giants than ADM, analysts said. Omaha, Neb.-based grain miller ConAgra Inc. began building four elevators in western Canada in October. Cargill Inc. and ADM both crush canola now.
As of last July, United Grain Growers owned 173 grain elevators in western Canada, down from 220 facilities a year earlier. The elevators handled 5.5 million metric tons of grain a year.
"UGG is an attractive partner for us in western Canada," ADM Chief Executive Allen Andreas said. "The company has some of the most modern and efficient grain handling facilities in Canada."

ADM owns, leases or has a 50 percent or greater interest in 276 processing plants, including 40 oilseed crushing plants worldwide, two of which are in Canada. ADM has 17 oilseed refineries, two in Canada, and 32 flour mills, 10 in Canada.
ADM also has four barley malting plants in the United States and one in Canada.

"Archer is very successfully expanding. Their ability to manage any type of grain-related facility is very good, so it looks like a win-win situation," said Leonard Teitelbaum, a Merrill Lynch food and agribusiness analyst.

Earlier this month, ADM agreed with Glencore Grain Holding to buy Glencore's grain facilities in Brazil and Paraguay, while last year ADM acquired Minneapolis grain merchandiser Benson-Quinn, which also operates actively in Canada.

The ADM stake in United Grain Growers comes after a bitter, hostile and unsuccessful takeover bid for UGG by Alberta Wheat Pool and Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, two big farmer-owned cooperatives, that was withdrawn March 18.
"This is a natural strategic fit between our two companies," UGG's Allen said.
